hypotheses.statement: Ambiguous similarity information (shared birthday) allows positive-mood participants to respond asymmetrically: assimilate to upward comparison targets, contrast from downward targets; without ambiguous information, responses are symmetric.

hypotheses.statement: Negative mood leads to symmetric (contrast) responses regardless of ambiguous-cue presence, ruling out a mood-congruent-processing account.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: the responses of participants in a negative mood were expected to be symmetric: contrast with both upward and downward comparison others

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving asymmetric responding in positive mood requires that similarity information be ambiguous; it should not occur when information is explicitly unambiguous.

hypotheses.statement: Cognitive load disrupts the effortful reinterpretation that produces self-serving asymmetric responding in positive mood, making load conditions resemble neutral-mood (symmetric assimilation) responses.

findings.quote: Experiment 1... Female university (N = 47) students participated in the study for monetary compensation. ... Exposure to the upward comparison target led to lowered self-evaluations (M = 3.33, SD = .65) compared to the downward comparison target (M = 4.64, SD = 1.50), F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011.

computed.derivation: For any independent two-group comparison drawn from a total sample of N participants, the maximum attainable error (denominator) df is N-2, because that value requires using every single participant as one of only two groups. With the paper's own stated N=47 for Experiment 1, max error df = 47-2 = 45. The paper reports F(1, 46), i.e. error df = 46, which requires n1+n2 >= 48 -- one more participant than the entire stated sample. This exceeds even the omnibus 2x2 model's own error df of 43 (also printed for this experiment, e.g. F(1,43)=38.80, F(1,43)=7.77, F(1,43)=5.99), which is itself already the largest error df attainable from a 4-cell model on N=47.

findings.notes: This is a pure counting argument (df cannot exceed N-2 for any subset of a fixed sample), verified against the paper's own explicitly stated N=47 and against the paper's own repeated use of df=43 for the omnibus model on this same experiment. The F statistic and p-value themselves are internally consistent (recalc_f_to_p on F(1,46)=6.95 gives p=.0114, matching the printed 'p = 011' i.e. p=.011), so the anomaly is specifically the printed denominator df, not the p-value arithmetic. An innocent explanation is a single-digit typographical slip (e.g., intended df=43, matching the rest of the experiment) rather than fabrication; language is kept to 'anomaly'/'inconsistency' per rulebook rule 9. This paper carries a journal retraction header and is documented (Levelt Committee) as containing fabricated data, which is relevant background but not itself evidence for this specific finding.

consequence.explanation: The df printed for this specific contrast (the paper's own demonstration that positive mood produces symmetric contrast responses in the absence of ambiguous similarity information) cannot have come from the stated N=47 sample under any two-group partition; the printed p-value is internally consistent with the (impossible) df as printed, so a reader cannot recover what the correct test actually was.

findings.location: Experiment 2 (Positive mood / Negative mood sections) and Experiment 4 (Manipulation check / No-load / Cognitive load sections)
findings.quote: As can be seen in Table 1, in the positive mood conditions, direction of comparison, F(1, 124) = 14.79, p < .001... Among the negative mood conditions, only the main effect of direction was significant, F(1, 124) = 56.97, p < .001.

computed.derivation: Experiment 2's own two explicit models are self-consistent: the 8-cell factorial-only omnibus ANOVA uses error df=118 (implying factorial N=126 and control n=141-126=15), and the model including the control condition as a 9th cell uses error df=132 (141-9=132, matching F(1,132)=340.44 for the manipulation check and the four control-contrast F(1,132) tests). Neither of those two internally-consistent models produces df=124. The identical literal value 124 is then reused, unexplained, for BOTH the positive-mood-only and negative-mood-only breakdown tests in Experiment 2, AND for the mood manipulation check and multiple control contrasts in Experiment 4 -- a completely different experiment with a different total N (193, not 141) and a different omnibus df (110, not 118).

findings.notes: Recurring identical denominator dfs across analyses that should generally have different degrees of freedom is the kind of too-good/repeated pattern flagged at low-moderate severity per rulebook rule 8. A legitimate explanation is that the authors used a pooled error term from an undocumented model (common in Jaccard 1998-style single-df contrast methods) that happens to coincide numerically -- the paper does not report enough information (per-cell or per-condition n) to reconstruct which model actually produces df=124, so this cannot be pushed to impossible; it is recorded as an unexplained reporting gap.

consequence.explanation: A reader cannot verify the denominator df used for the paper's key simple-effects breakdowns (the tests that support the asymmetric-responding claim in both Experiments 2 and 4), because it matches no model the paper otherwise documents.

findings.notes: Both tables report mean (SD) on stated, printable Likert scales (self-evaluation: 1-7 single item; similarity: 1-9 three-item composite), which would ordinarily make GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE (for self-evaluation) directly applicable -- but NEITHER table, nor the surrounding participants paragraphs, states a per-cell or per-condition n anywhere in the paper. This is recorded as a genuine coverage gap (a 'no per-cell n reported' pattern across all four experiments) rather than as an anomaly about the authors, though it is worth noting that this is exactly the reporting gap that would make the most powerful checks (GRIM/GRIMMER on stated-scale single-item means) inapplicable to this paper.
